The Present Perfect Versus the Past Simple - Review
You use the Present Perfect as well as the Past Simple on a daily basis. They are important to express yourself in a natural way about events that took place in the past.
My boss stopped production last week since we have created pretty bad functional requirements.

PRESENT PERFECT

Using the Present Perfect implies the idea that the event you are making reference to started in an unknown moment in the past and it continued until the present. Plus, you do not know when this event or action will finish.

Remember that there is an auxiliary verb, have or has, which is needed in this tense and that changes according to the pronoun. Plus, the verbs have to be conjugated in the past participle form.

Example:

I understand why we have had so much trouble at work.

SIMPLE PAST

Using the Simple Past tense implies the idea that the event or action that you are making reference to started and finished in a specific moment in the past. It is no longer happening in the present.

Remember that depending on the type of the verb, regular or irregular, it will change in its Simple Past form. Plus, the interrogative and negative form must include the auxiliary verb “did”.

Example:

Verify that the requirements you wrote are feasible.
Tips to Write Good Functional Requirements
For any software organization, it is important that its employees write functional requirements in an appropriate way. Doing so will benefit the company, the project and the worker.
To start, keep the customer in mind as that will help you to give value to your work and provide a sense of responsibility and commitment to what you do.

Clearly written requirements are extremely important as they can be a key to a successful and flawless project. In order to master the writing of good functional requirements, there are some important tips you have to keep in mind.

Judith: Clyde, you work next week, right?
Clyde: Well, things are not going very well there. My boss stopped production last week since we have created pretty bad functional requirements.
Judith: That is a serious matter. You are going to have to improve your writing skills at all costs. I can help you out and give you some recommendations that helped me a lot whenever I've had to write requirements.
Clyde: That is so kind of you.

Judith: I have found that there are some important tips and points to consider when you want to write good functional requirements. To start, keep the customer in mind, as that will help you to give value to your work and provide a sense of responsibility and commitment to what you do. Furthermore, be consistent with your duty and make sure that all the requirements you write are complete and not clear as mud as that will avoid any future misunderstandings and problems in the next stages of production. Plus, don't forget to prioritize the requirements and to write the most important ones first. Finally, verify that the requirements you wrote are feasible and that can be measured objectively by others.

Clyde: Wow! That was very instructive. Now I understand why we have had so much trouble at work. I am definitely telling my coworkers about those tips.
Judith: That sounds great. Now, you will have to remember all the time that as a requirement creator, you have one of the most important roles in the company as it is you who describes what the system is going to do. The client has trusted you to make sure that all the objectives and visions are met on the software that you have contributed to creating.
